You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: In the edited image, is the woman's jacket fully closed, with its front panels together and no visible opening remaining along the closure?
node.criteria: Pass: the jacket is visibly fully closed, with its front panels together and no opening along the closure. Fail: the jacket is visibly not fully closed, including any visible opening along the closure. Unknown: the closure or its full extent cannot be judged from the image.
node.binding: Directly inspect the requested endpoint in the edited image; the input image is context for identifying the woman's jacket, not a prerequisite for checking the endpoint.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows the woman's jacket hanging open, with a clear gap between the front panels.
The edited image shows the jacket hanging open, with a clear gap between its front panels.
The jacket is visibly open in the edited image, with its front panels separated and a large opening remaining.

fulfillment: The node is structurally wired and repeatedly executes validly, so this is not a transport, schema, or dependency failure. The traces consistently describe the edited jacket as open, but the supplied edited image shows the woman turned sideways with the bright pink jacket swinging outward; that view does not clearly establish whether its front closure is fully fastened. The source also shows the jacket front partly obscured, so a confident claim of no progress from direct comparison is not well supported. Treat closure and change-versus-source as separate visual judgments: require clear evidence for a fully closed endpoint, and mark progress unresolved when pose, occlusion, or garment motion prevents a reliable comparison. Do not convert uncertainty into a negative finding. The five repeated high-confidence ‘no’ outputs are an investigation signal, not proof that the requested edit is absent; inspect whether the checks are mistaking the flared silhouette for an open closure, while retaining the rubric’s completion and partial-progress criteria.
s2: The node is validly wired and repeatedly executes, so do not change transport, schema, or dependencies. Its main weakness is conflating a flared, swinging jacket silhouette with an unfastened front: in the edited image the woman is turned sideways and the bright pink jacket hangs outward, while the source front is also partly obscured. Tighten the visual criterion to inspect the actual front closure/panel alignment and compare corresponding visible regions, rather than treating the jacket’s outline or a visible gap alone as proof of no progress. Keep endpoint completion distinct from partial progress: this node should pass only on discernible change toward closure that remains incomplete, fail only when comparable evidence supports no change, and return unknown when pose, occlusion, or motion prevents that comparison. Preserve the rubric’s full-closure and partial-progress checks; the repeated high-confidence failures are a reason to investigate this ambiguity, not grounds to force a positive label.
